The Arithmetic Logic Unit

Every add, compare, and bitwise decision a computer makes passes through one small circuit. This exhibit opens up the ALU — the block that turns two binary numbers and an opcode into a result and a set of flags — and lets you operate one yourself.

01 · Anatomy

Two operands, one opcode, one answer

Operands — A & B

The two binary numbers the ALU acts on. In a real CPU these arrive from registers; here, you'll set them yourself with the switches below.

Opcode

A short binary instruction from the control unit that tells the ALU which operation to run — add, subtract, AND, shift, and so on.

Result & flags

The output bus carries the answer. Alongside it, four status flags — Zero, Carry, Negative, Overflow — report facts about that answer the rest of the CPU can branch on.

02 · Operations

The instruction set

Each card is a datasheet for one operation the ALU can run. Open one for its truth table and gate-level view.

ADD 0000

Addition +

Binary addition with carry-out, built from a chain of full adders.
SUB 0001

Subtraction −

Reuses the adder by inverting B and adding 1 — two's complement in action.
AND 0100

Bitwise AND ∧

One AND gate per bit position — used constantly to mask off bits.
XOR 0110

Bitwise XOR ⊕

Outputs 1 when its inputs differ — the basis of bit-flipping and comparison.
SHL 1000

Shift Left ≪

Slides every bit one place left, dropping the top bit into Carry.

05 · Adder Circuits Compared

Ripple Carry vs. Carry Lookahead

RCA

Ripple Carry Adder

Each Full Adder waits for the carry-out from the previous stage before computing its sum bit.

Advantages

  • Simple circuit design
  • Fewer logic gates
  • Easy to implement

Trade-offs

  • Slow — each carry must ripple forward
  • Delay grows linearly with bit width
CLA

Carry Lookahead Adder

Uses Generate (G) and Propagate (P) signals to calculate all carry values simultaneously before summing.

Advantages

  • Fast — all carries computed at once
  • Constant delay (independent of width)
  • Used in real CPUs

Trade-offs

  • More complex circuitry
  • Higher gate count
  • More wiring overhead

How Subtraction Works: Two's Complement

Instead of building a separate subtraction circuit, the ALU reuses the adder. To compute A − B, it calculates A + (−B). In binary, the negative of a number is its two's complement: flip all bits (~B), then add 1.

Step 1: Original B B = 0011 (3)
Step 2: Invert all bits ~B = 1100
Step 3: Add 1 (carry-in = 1) ~B + 1 = 1101 (-3)

In the simulator, when SUB is selected, Operand B is automatically inverted and the initial carry-in is set to 1 — exactly replicating this hardware behavior.

04 · How it got here

From relays to silicon

  1. 1937–44

    Relay logic

    Electromechanical relays open and close to perform binary addition — slow, audible, and the first machines to compute with switches instead of gears.

  2. 1945

    Vacuum-tube arithmetic

    ENIAC's accumulators add and subtract using thousands of tubes, trading relay speed limits for heat and constant tube failures.

  3. 1958–63

    Discrete transistors

    Transistorized logic shrinks the arithmetic unit onto circuit boards small enough to fit inside a single cabinet.

  4. 1970

    The 74181 IC

    A single 24-pin chip packages a full 4-bit ALU — sixteen arithmetic and logic operations selectable by four control lines.

  5. 1971–today

    Embedded in the CPU

    From the Intel 4004 onward, the ALU stops being a separate unit and becomes a block on the processor's own die.
